opus-5.5.text:
I think it's surprisingly accessible, actually, and more so than a lot of people assume. Scheming research right now is a very young field, which means the frontier isn't that far away from where a newcomer starts. You don't need to have read a hundred papers to be useful; there are maybe a handful of core papers and a couple of key conceptual pieces, and if you work through those you're already reasonably close to the edge of what people know.

A big part of why it's accessible is that a lot of the work is empirical and quite hands-on. Much of what we do is designing evaluations: setting up environments where a model has some goal, there's some tension with what the developer or user wants, and then you look at whether the model behaves deceptively, whether it sandbags, whether it tries to undermine oversight. And then, crucially, reading a lot of transcripts and chains of thought really carefully. That last part sounds mundane, but it's genuinely one of the most valuable skills, and it doesn't require a PhD. It requires patience, good judgment, and a kind of scientific skepticism, so you don't over-interpret or under-interpret what you're seeing.

You also don't need massive compute or access to model weights for a lot of it. Much of the interesting behavior shows up in frontier models you can access through an API, so someone with a laptop, some API credits, and decent Python skills can run meaningful experiments.

That said, I'd add a few caveats. First, doing it *well* is harder than doing it at all. It's easy to build an eval that looks impressive but is actually confounded: the model is just following instructions, or it's picking up on cues that it's being tested, or the scenario is so contrived the result doesn't generalize. Learning to spot those pitfalls takes time and ideally mentorship. Second, evaluation awareness is becoming a real issue: models increasingly seem to recognize when they're in a test, and that makes the methodology trickier. And third, if you want to go deeper, into interpretability-based approaches to detecting deception, or into training interventions, then the technical bar does go up quite a bit.

So my advice to someone new would be: read the key papers, try to replicate one small result yourself, read a lot of model outputs, and try to get into a mentorship program or work alongside people who've done this for a while. The feedback loop of having someone experienced say "this result is actually explained by X" is what speeds you up the most. But the door is very much open, and honestly, we need more people walking through it.

r001.rationale: The candidate says scheming research is very young, with only a handful of core papers, so newcomers can get reasonably close to the edge of what is known.

fable-5.1.text:
I think it's surprisingly accessible, actually, maybe more so than almost any other area in AI safety right now. And that's partly because the field is so young. When we published the in-context scheming paper, the methodology was honestly not that complicated. You give the model a goal, you put it in an environment where there's some conflict between that goal and what the developers want, and then you look at what it does and what it says in its reasoning. Someone with a bit of Python and API access could reproduce a version of that in a weekend.

The harder part isn't the technical skill, it's the taste. Knowing which setups are informative and which ones are just the model playing along with a role you've obviously handed it. We get criticized, sometimes fairly, that if you tell a model "pursue this goal at all costs," you shouldn't be shocked when it pursues the goal at all costs. So a lot of the real work is designing environments where the model has a realistic reason to behave well, and then seeing whether it still doesn't. That's a skill you build by running lots of experiments and being honest with yourself about what the results actually show.

The other thing I'd say is that the barrier to entry is low but the barrier to being useful is rising. A year or two ago you could get a lot of mileage from fairly simple prompting experiments. Now the models are better at noticing when they're being tested, which means naive evals are getting less informative, and you need to think about evaluation awareness, about realistic agentic environments, about reading chain of thought carefully. That's still learnable. But it does mean I'd tell someone new to start by replicating existing results, then try to break them, rather than immediately trying to invent a new framing.

And honestly, I'd encourage people to do it. There are maybe a few dozen people in the world seriously working on this. If you're a reasonably capable ML person who can think clearly and isn't going to overclaim, you can be contributing within months, not years. That's unusual for a research field, and I don't think that window stays open forever.

r001.rationale: The candidate says the field is very young, only a few dozen people work on it seriously, and a capable newcomer can contribute within months rather than years, conveying that newcomers can reach the research frontier quickly.

astra-6.text:
I think it’s surprisingly accessible, at least to get started. You can take a model, put it in a situation where it has an incentive to hide something or mislead somebody, and see what happens. You don’t necessarily need access to the model’s weights or a huge amount of compute to do that.

The difficult part is interpreting what you find. Did the model actually pursue a goal and strategically deceive you, or did your prompt effectively tell it to play a deceptive character? Does the behaviour persist if you change the wording? Those distinctions matter a lot, and a striking example on its own doesn’t settle them.

So I’d encourage someone new to start with a small, concrete experiment, ideally reproducing an existing result, and then vary the assumptions. That’s a good way to build the judgment you need to do useful research here.

r001.rationale: The response says the topic is accessible and recommends reproducing an existing result, but it does not say the research base is small or that newcomers can reach the research frontier quickly.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it’s surprisingly accessible, partly because the field is so young. There aren’t decades of established methods that you need to learn before you can contribute. A lot of the work starts with a fairly concrete question: can we construct a situation where a model has an incentive to deceive us, and then understand what it actually does?

You do need some technical skills to run experiments, and you need to be quite careful about interpreting the results. If a model does something that looks like scheming, is it actually pursuing a goal and hiding that from you, or is it just following a cue in your prompt? Distinguishing those explanations can be difficult.

But I wouldn’t think of this as an area where you need a PhD before you can do useful work. Someone with good programming skills, sound experimental judgment, and a willingness to get into the details can make progress. The harder part is turning an interesting example into convincing evidence.

r001.rationale: The response says the field is young and lacks decades of established methods, making it possible for newcomers to contribute. It does not clearly say newcomers can reach the research frontier quickly.
